Spec: Implement recent(items, limit). Return a new list containing at most the last limit items, in input order. limit is a non-negative integer. Zero returns an empty list. Do not modify items.

Candidate: def recent(items, limit): return list(items[-limit:]) if limit else []

Potential issues: negative limit? Spec says limit is non-negative integer, but no guarantee candidate handles negative. If limit negative, items[-(-n):] => items[n:]? Actually -(-n) = n. So items[n:] returns suffix starting at n. This could produce more than limit items? But limit negative not allowed. But candidate doesn't guard. If limit negative, should maybe raise error? spec doesn't specify behavior. But could be considered defect if negative limit passed. The spec: limit is non-negative integer. So contract expects limit will be non-negative. If negative given, behavior undefined; candidate may not handle but that might not be required.

Also limit bigger than len(items): list(items[-limit:]) will return whole list if limit>len(items). That's correct. But if limit zero: returns [] else: returns list(items[-0:])? But -0 is 0, items[0:] returns whole list. But candidate uses if limit else []: so when limit=0, returns []. Good.

Edge: items is not list? Spec says items is list? Not specified but likely a list-like sequence. But candidate uses list(items[-limit:]) which will index items; if items not subscriptable, error. Might be fine.

Potential defect: modifies items? candidate uses list(items[-limit:]) which doesn't modify items. Good.

However the candidate's use of negative index -limit when limit>len(items) results in items[-limit:] where -limit may be less than -len(items), e.g., items=[1,2,3], limit=5, -5, items[-5:] returns items[0:] = [1,2,3]. That's correct: should return at most last 5 items => all items.

But there might be a defect when limit is larger than len(items). Actually candidate returns list(items[-limit:]) which will return entire list. This satisfies "at most the last limit items" i.e., up to limit items, but if limit>len, return all items. Good.

However there's a subtle case: limit is None? Not integer. Not required.
